opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the natural starting point is the trend METR has been tracking: the length of tasks, measured in how long they take a skilled human, that AI agents can complete at some reliability threshold, like 50%. Historically that's been doubling roughly every seven months, and more recently it looks like it's been going faster, maybe closer to every four to five months. If you naively extrapolate the faster trend, you'd expect something like two to three doublings over the next year. So if we're currently at tasks that take a human a few hours, you'd end up at tasks that take a human somewhere between a day and a week, at 50% reliability.

I think that's roughly my median, with a bunch of caveats. One is that the 50% reliability number is a bit flattering. If you look at 80% reliability, the horizon is a lot shorter, often by a factor of four or five. So "can sometimes do a week-long task" is quite different from "can reliably be handed a week-long task and you trust the result."

Another caveat is that these benchmark tasks are cleaner than real software engineering. They're well-specified, self-contained, and checkable. Real work involves messy codebases, ambiguous requirements, and judgment about what "done" means. So I'd expect real-world usefulness to lag the benchmark numbers somewhat, though the gap might shrink as companies train specifically on more realistic agentic environments.

On the upside, there are reasons the trend could go faster than extrapolation. Labs are pouring a lot of effort into RL on long-horizon agentic tasks, and that seems to be paying off. There's also a dynamic where once agents get good enough at the kinds of tasks AI researchers themselves do, you start getting some acceleration of AI R&D itself. I don't think that's a huge effect over the next year, but it pushes in that direction.

On the downside, it's possible we hit a wall where longer tasks require qualitatively different skills, like maintaining coherent plans over many hours, recovering from errors, and knowing when to step back, and that those don't come for free from scaling current methods. I put real weight on that, but I don't think the evidence so far points strongly toward it.

So my overall picture: probably two to three more doublings, landing in the range of tasks that take humans a day or a few days, with meaningful probability of faster progress and also meaningful probability that things stall somewhat. I'd be pretty surprised if we didn't see at least one more doubling.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects two to three doublings over the next year, but does not forecast a doubling time of roughly two to four months; it describes the recent pace as four to five months.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the historical pace was roughly seven months and the recent pace four to five months. It does not suggest a longer-run doubling time of roughly six months.

fable-5.1.text:
Ryan Greenblatt: So the way I'd frame this is in terms of the METR time horizon metric, which is basically: take a bunch of software engineering tasks, look at how long they take human experts, and ask at what task length the AI succeeds 50% of the time. Historically that's been doubling roughly every seven months over the long run, and more like every four months if you look at the recent period.

My default expectation over the next year is that the trend continues at something like the faster recent rate, maybe a bit slower. So if we're currently at tasks that take skilled humans a few hours, I'd guess a year from now we're at something like a full day or two of expert work at 50% reliability. That's roughly two to four doublings. I'd put most of my probability mass in that range, and I'd be fairly surprised if it was less than one doubling or more than, say, five.

A few caveats I'd flag, though. One is that the 50% reliability number can be misleading. For actually substituting for an engineer, you care more about the 80% horizon, and that lags behind by a meaningful factor, maybe four or five times shorter. So "a day of work at 50%" might mean "a couple of hours of work you can actually trust."

The second is that these benchmark tasks are cleaner than real work. They're well-specified, self-contained, and the model gets clear feedback. Real engineering involves ambiguity, messy codebases, and tacit context. So I'd expect real-world task length to be increasing, but I'm less confident the translation is one-to-one. That said, I think the gap has been closing as labs put more effort into agentic training specifically.

And then the bigger-picture point: the reason I care about this is that if the trend holds for several more years, you get to horizons of weeks or months, and at that point you're talking about AIs that could plausibly automate a large fraction of AI research itself. So the next year is partly interesting as a test of whether the faster trend is real or whether we're seeing a temporary burst from labs targeting this capability directly. I lean towards it being substantially real, but I hold maybe 25 or 30% on things slowing noticeably, either because of compute scaling constraints or because the easy gains from RL on agentic tasks get used up.

r001.rationale: The response cites a recent historical pace of about four months, but its forecast is less specific: it expects that pace or somewhat slower and gives a range of two to four doublings over the year. It does not clearly forecast a doubling every two to four months.

r002.rationale: It says the long-run doubling pace has been roughly every seven months, which is a reasonable approximation of six months.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect it to increase substantially, but I’m pretty uncertain about the rate. One way to frame this is: how long would a task take a human software engineer, and what fraction of tasks of that length can the AI complete? That’s different from how long you can leave the AI running. It might run for hours without making much useful progress.

You can get fairly large increases in task length from improvements that look modest on shorter tasks. If the model becomes better at noticing when it’s stuck, testing its work, and recovering from mistakes, that can let it sustain useful progress for much longer.

So over the next year, I’d expect tasks that currently require substantial supervision to become feasible with much less intervention. But I wouldn’t assume that translates directly into being able to hand an AI an arbitrary week-long engineering project. Real projects involve ambiguous requirements, unfamiliar codebases, and decisions about what’s worth doing. Reliability on those dimensions could lag behind performance on well-specified tasks.

r001.rationale: The response expects substantial growth but says it is uncertain about the rate; it does not forecast doubling every two to four months.

r002.rationale: The response gives no roughly six-month doubling-time estimate.

sol-6.1.text:
My best guess is that the length of tasks they can do will increase by something like a factor of five over the next year, though I’m pretty uncertain. A factor of two or a factor of ten wouldn’t be that surprising to me.

One thing that makes this tricky is what we mean by “can complete.” Is it a task they succeed at half the time, or one you can reliably hand off and expect to get done? And are we measuring on fairly self-contained tasks, where there’s a clear test of success, or on work that requires figuring out what someone actually wants?

I’d expect substantial progress on the self-contained tasks. But I wouldn’t immediately translate that into “you can leave the AI working for a week and come back to a useful result.” There’s a difference between occasionally succeeding on a long task and being dependable enough that delegating it saves you time.

r001.rationale: It forecasts about a fivefold increase over the year, with twofold or tenfold also plausible, but gives no doubling interval of two to four months.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a longer-run trend or a roughly six-month doubling time.
